lesson.title: What Gas Pressure Really Is
lesson.summary: Gas pressure comes from countless molecular collisions with a container's walls; this section explains the mechanism behind pressure and shows how to calculate it for a sample of gas.
lesson.body:
You already know that a gas is made of particles moving freely and rapidly through the space available to them, colliding with each other and with anything that bounds that space. Gas pressure is simply what those collisions add up to: every time a molecule strikes a wall, it delivers a tiny push, and the combined effect of billions of such pushes per second, spread over the wall's area, is what you measure as pressure. Pressure is defined as force per unit area, so anything that changes how hard or how often molecules hit the walls will change the pressure you observe.

Three things control that collision rate and force, and it helps to reason through each one separately. First, if you pack more molecules into the same container, there are simply more particles available to strike the walls at any given moment, so pressure rises. Second, if you raise the temperature, the molecules move faster on average, which means they hit the walls both more often and with greater force per collision, so pressure rises again. Third, if you increase the volume while keeping the same number of molecules at the same temperature, those molecules now have farther to travel between collisions and more wall area to be spread across, so collisions become less frequent per unit area and pressure drops. Notice that pressure isn't a property of individual molecules ,  it's a statistical result of enormous numbers of collisions happening every instant.

These three relationships combine into a single quantitative expression you'll use throughout this chapter: P = nRT/V, where n is the amount of gas in moles, T is the absolute temperature, V is the container's volume, and R is a constant that keeps the units consistent. For now, treat this as a bookkeeping tool for turning the qualitative picture above into a number, rather than something you need to derive.

Here's how it plays out with real numbers. Suppose you seal 0.040 mol of a gas into a rigid 1.0 L container at 300 K. Using R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K), the pressure works out to P = (0.040 mol)(0.08206 L·atm/mol·K)(300 K) / (1.0 L), which comes to about 0.98 atm. Physically, that number reflects a fixed population of molecules, moving with kinetic energy set by 300 K, confined to a fairly small volume ,  enough collisions per second, at that container's wall area, to produce just under one atmosphere of push.

It's worth pausing on why doubling the volume, say to 2.0 L, would cut this pressure roughly in half rather than leaving it unchanged. The same 0.040 mol of gas at the same temperature is still colliding just as energetically, but now those collisions are distributed over a larger volume, so any given patch of wall gets struck less frequently. Pressure, in other words, is never just about how much gas you have ,  it always depends jointly on how much space that gas is squeezed into and how energetically its molecules are moving.
